proposedTopics.title: Hardhat 3
proposedTopics.description: Hardhat 3 is the secondary toolchain in this curriculum: Ignition deployment modules, network/config management, plugins, typed TypeScript integrations, and Foundry-compatible Solidity tests used where a JS/frontend workflow matters.

proposedTopics.title: Hardhat 3 project setup
proposedTopics.description: A Hardhat 3 project is a Node/TS package whose root hardhat.config.ts defines compiler and network settings, plugins, tasks, and optional path overrides. npx hardhat --init scaffolds a working project, and Hardhat 3 supports Solidity tests alongside plugin-provided TypeScript test runners.

proposedTopics.title: Hardhat Ignition deployment
proposedTopics.description: Ignition is Hardhat's declarative deployment system: a module declares contract instances and operations, Ignition derives their execution order, runs independent transactions in parallel, records deployment results, and can recover or resume without repeating completed work.

requirements.purpose: Declare and deploy an Ignition module, then verify that a rerun recognizes completed deployment work

Done when: deployment succeeds and re-running the same command reports no pending deployment actions.

proposedTopics.title: Network & config management
proposedTopics.description: hardhat.config.ts maps network names to in-memory edr-simulated networks or http JSON-RPC connections. Simulated networks can fork a URL and pin a block; configuration variables defer RPC URL and key lookup so sensitive values are not hardcoded in committed config.

proposedTopics.title: Hardhat plugins ecosystem
proposedTopics.description: Hardhat's plugin system composes optional capabilities such as viem integration, assertion helpers, test runners, Ignition, verification, and Foundry-remapping compatibility. A configured plugin may add tasks, hooks, configuration fields, or runtime extensions, so the installed and configured set defines the project's usable surfaces.

proposedTopics.title: Coexisting: shared remappings + .t.sol tests
proposedTopics.description: Hardhat 3 natively loads scoped remappings.txt files from a project and imported npm packages; Foundry projects that rely on Forge-autogenerated remappings can add the official hardhat-foundry plugin. Hardhat also runs Foundry-origin Solidity tests within its documented compatibility surface, so a supported .t.sol test and source tree can serve both runners while each tool keeps its own config.

proposedTopics.title: When to reach for Foundry vs Hardhat
proposedTopics.description: Choose by the required surface, not by an outdated Solidity-versus-JavaScript split: use Forge for curriculum tasks that explicitly exercise Forge-specific testing and analysis commands; use Hardhat for Ignition deployments, viem-facing TypeScript integration, or its plugin ecosystem. Hardhat 3 itself supports Solidity unit, fuzz, and invariant tests, and TypeScript tests can run alongside them.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does hardhat.config.ts declare, and what testing option does Hardhat 3 add that Hardhat 2 didn't have?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The Solidity compiler version/settings, source/test paths, and networks. Hardhat 3 adds first-class Foundry-compatible Solidity tests (.t.sol, forge-std style) alongside the original TypeScript test runner. Pitfall: both test styles still compile from ONE shared contracts/ tree — a config mistake there breaks both.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Complete Speedrun Ethereum challenges 0–2 (Simple NFT Example, Decentralized Staking App, Token Vendor).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Each challenge scaffolds a Scaffold-ETH 2 (Hardhat-based) project with a contract plus a Next.js frontend; deploy locally with Hardhat, pass the contract's own test suite, then follow the challenge's deploy/verify steps.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why write a TS integration test with viem in addition to a Foundry Solidity test for the same contract?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A TS test exercises the viem-facing ABI, typing, accounts, and multi-contract wiring used by clients and scripts, complementing contract-internal Solidity tests. Use each style for the boundary it can actually observe instead of assuming one runner replaces the other.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a viem-based Hardhat TS test deploying a contract and asserting a read call.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: import assert from "node:assert/strict"; const counter = await viem.deployContract("Counter"); await counter.write.increment(); assert.equal(await counter.read.count(), 1n);

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Ignition's deployment journal let you safely do that a plain imperative deploy script can't?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Resume a partially-failed multi-contract deployment without re-deploying contracts that already succeeded, because Ignition tracks what's been deployed against a module's declared dependency graph. Pitfall: Ignition modules are declarative, so imperative control flow (loops/conditionals over deploys) doesn't work the way a hand-written script would.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a minimal Hardhat Ignition module deploying a Counter with a constructor arg of 0.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: import { buildModule } from "@nomicfoundation/hardhat-ignition/modules"; export default buildModule("Phase03", (m) => { const counter = m.contract("Counter", [0]); return { counter }; });

proposedPrompts.promptText: What's the difference between an edr-simulated network and an http network in Hardhat 3's config, and why keep RPC URLs as configuration variables?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: edr-simulated runs an in-memory local chain (optionally forking a real one); http points at a real JSON-RPC endpoint. Configuration variables keep secrets (RPC URLs, keys) out of the committed hardhat.config.ts. Pitfall: a forking config still needs a valid url — without one, forking is disabled.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does a Hardhat plugin actually add to a project, beyond 'more npm packages'?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A plugin can add CLI tasks, hooks, config fields, global options, or runtime extensions (for example, hardhat-viem exposes viem helpers on a network connection). Check the installed plugin's documented capability instead of assuming every plugin adds every kind of surface.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Hardhat 3 actually read to resolve a remapped Solidity import, and what does it NOT parse directly?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Hardhat 3 natively loads scoped remappings.txt files from the project and imported npm packages. If a Foundry project relies on Forge-autogenerated remappings instead, add @nomicfoundation/hardhat-foundry; otherwise an import can resolve under Forge but fail under Hardhat.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why can a Foundry .t.sol test run unmodified under Hardhat's own test runner, without either tool 'owning' it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Hardhat treats Solidity files under test/ as tests and .t.sol files under contracts/ as tests, supports forge-std, and can execute Foundry-origin tests within its documented compatibility surface. The source can be shared, but generated test artifacts and compiler settings remain tool-specific.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: When to reach for Foundry vs Hardhat
proposedPrompts.promptText: Give the one-line decision rule for choosing Foundry vs Hardhat for a given task in this curriculum.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Use Forge when the task specifically needs Forge commands or analysis; use Hardhat for Ignition, viem-facing TypeScript integration, or a Hardhat plugin surface. Hardhat 3 also runs Solidity unit/fuzz/invariant tests, so choose from the concrete workflow rather than an old language-only split.
